candidates.title: Multi-agent Scaling Across Disjunctive and Compensatory Tasks
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.AI primary, cs.MA cross-list; not yet peer reviewed)
candidates.citationVelocity: unable to confirm via Semantic Scholar (429 rate limited after 3 retries); submitted 2026-09-25, 4 days old, near-zero is the reasonable inference
candidates.institution: Jozef Stefan Institute, Ljubljana, Slovenia (Carolina Fortuna, Blaz Bertalanic -- the same pair has a directly related prior conference paper on multi-agent debate consensus, May 2026, confirmed via ResearchGate/Google Scholar profiles)
communitySignals: not found in sampled HuggingFace Daily Papers
code listed in the paper itself as '[Open code placeholder]' -- not yet publicly released
no Papers with Code entry found
credibilityEvidence: Section 3.1-3.2: 13 open-weight models (3B-20B), team sizes {1,2,3,5,7,10,15,20,25,30}, ~6.8x10^7 total per-agent generations across 5 disjunctive benchmarks (GSM8K, GSM-Hard, MATH-500, MMLU-Hard, ARC-Challenge) plus 1 compensatory benchmark (RealFP Fermi problems)

Section 3.3: theoretical model (Proposition 2.1, task-type scaling under correlation and bias) validated against observed data -- predicted vs observed plurality-voting accuracy differ by 0.48 points on average across 650 model-task-team-size configurations (Pearson r=0.999)

Section 3.4: compensatory-task error decomposition validated to within 0.6% average error across 10 models (Pearson r=0.997); item-level bias explicitly measured and separated from within-item variance
Section 3.3/3.4: heterogeneous-team ablations (5-model pools, best-of-8-choose-5 selected on held-out splits) reported with explicit comparison against each pool's strongest single member
temperature-invariance check (T in {0.4,0.8,1.0}) reported as a robustness control
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers the theoretical mechanism, large-scale empirical validation across 13 models and 2 task regimes, per-model breakdowns, and heterogeneous-team ablations with statistically tight model fit; does not yet include closed frontier models (GPT/Claude/Gemini) or team sizes beyond 30
reproducibilityEvidence: paper explicitly marks code as '[Open code placeholder]' in the abstract -- not yet public at the time of this screening
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The scoped claim (task structure, not team size alone, determines multi-agent scaling behavior) is supported by a theoretical model whose predictions match observed data to within fractions of a percentage point across hundreds of configurations
candidates.primaryLimitation: Only tests 13 open-weight models (3B-20B); does not include frontier closed models where production multi-agent systems are most often deployed, and the code is not yet public so independent verification is not currently possible
candidates.presentationReason: Theory, experimental setup, and per-regime results are laid out with explicit equations, named benchmarks, and tables; the paper is upfront that code is not yet released
candidates.reason: Selected: gives teams a concrete, validated way to predict whether adding agents to a task will help at all, before building the multi-agent system -- directly actionable for anyone deciding between single-agent and multi-agent architectures

candidates.title: AgentWorld: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Collaboration of Multi-agent LLMs
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.MA; not yet peer reviewed)
candidates.citationVelocity: 0 citations in 1 day (confirmed via Semantic Scholar)
candidates.institution: Columbia University, University of Pennsylvania, Seoul National University, Penn State University, with the OpenAgents open-source community contributing task annotation
communitySignals: not found in sampled HuggingFace Daily Papers
fully open-source: GitHub repo (github.com/openagents-org/agentworld) plus project website agentworld.io, confirmed live via GitHub API
annotation and evaluation effort credited to OpenAgents community volunteers
credibilityEvidence: Section 3-4: 100 human-annotated tasks + 100 LLM-augmented variants, 3-20 agents, 25-55 round budgets, evaluated on 4 frontier models (Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5 Mini, DeepSeek R1-70B) under identical prompts/tools
Section 4.4: 5 explicit baselines (random actions, single-agent-does-everything, no-communication, shared-plan-no-communication, oracle-communication) isolating what collaboration itself contributes

Section 4.4: design-component ablation on a 35-task subset (removing role info, shortening horizon, randomizing spawn, withholding documentation) plus a 3-seed run-to-run variance check (SD 0.0 percentage points on SR)

Section 4.3: the paper's own CCE metric validated against 84 independent human causal judgments (Cohen's kappa=0.64, comparable to inter-judge-model kappa=0.66 on 7,298 decisions) and shown robust across 3 different judge models
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers main results, baselines that isolate the effect being measured, ablations, run-to-run variance, and independent human validation of the novel metric -- unusually thorough for a benchmark paper introducing a new environment and a new metric in the same release
reproducibilityEvidence: GitHub repo publishes the full sandbox, task definitions with verifiers, evaluation scripts, and the data-annotation platform (confirmed live via GitHub API)
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The scoped claim (current frontier models cap out around 52% success and waste most of their actions on long-horizon multi-agent collaboration tasks) is backed by baselines that rule out simpler explanations (task difficulty alone, low-level control burden) and a human-validated metric
candidates.primaryLimitation: Only 4 primary frontier models tested (DeepSeek R1-70B is a smaller/older model than the other three, which weakens the cross-model comparison); on the augmented (harder) task variants every model's success rate roughly halves, suggesting some of the benchmark's headline numbers may still be sensitive to exact task phrasing
candidates.presentationReason: Environment design, task design rationale, metric formalization, and all ablations are documented with explicit numbers and a public appendix
candidates.reason: Selected: the first benchmark to isolate genuine long-horizon collaboration from both task difficulty and low-level action control, with a human-validated metric showing the best model wastes over two-thirds of its actions -- a concrete ceiling for anyone building multi-agent systems today

candidates.title: Towards Mitigating Fabricated Consensus: The Active Provenance Gate for Multi-Agent Debate Synthesis
candidates.venue: Accepted, 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026) -- peer-reviewed
candidates.citationVelocity: unable to confirm via Semantic Scholar (429 rate limited after 2 retries); submitted 2026-09-25, 4 days old, near-zero is the reasonable inference
candidates.institution: Institute of Computer Science, Warsaw University of Technology, Poland
communitySignals: not found in sampled HuggingFace Daily Papers
no Papers with Code entry found
public GitHub repo (github.com/m-Jakub/resilient-mas-framework) with a dedicated reproducibility bundle for this paper, confirmed live via GitHub API
credibilityEvidence: Section IV-V: 90 adversarial runs on a knowledge-grounded crisis-simulation corpus (kg_cfr_full), reporting Provenance Fidelity (PF, sentence-level NLI-entailment ratio) before and after the gate, plus divergence rates under high vs low epistemic conflict

Section V-B: validator-symmetry ablation -- using the same model as both generator and NLI auditor wrongly approved unsafe compromises 85.6% of the time; switching to an asymmetric stronger-model validator reduced this substantially, with explicit before/after numbers
Section IV: blind A/B human study (N=33) with a paired t-test on calibrated trust (t(32)=3.12, p=0.0039) in the highest-conflict scenario

authors explicitly disclose limitations: synthetic simulation only, closed-world provenance assumption (checked against the debate corpus, not external reality), small human-study N, and LLM-judge circularity risk
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: The core grounding mechanism (PF measurement, self-healing, hard gate) is tested with reasonable rigor and a real peer-reviewed venue, but the evaluation is confined to one synthetic crisis-simulation testbed and a 33-person convenience-sample human study, so generalization to real production multi-agent debate systems is not yet demonstrated
reproducibilityEvidence: GitHub repo publishes the debate corpus, full prompt templates, the complete verification codebase, and the human-study survey data (confirmed live via GitHub API)
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The narrow claim (an explicit post-debate verification gate reduces fabricated consensus and that users prefer an honest failure report over a fluent fake one in high-conflict cases) is supported by a peer-reviewed, statistically significant result, but the small human-study sample and single synthetic domain mean the practical magnitude in real deployments is still open
candidates.presentationReason: Architecture, formalization of Provenance Fidelity, experimental setup, and limitations are all explicitly laid out, including an honest discussion of the LLM-judge circularity risk
candidates.reason: Selected: multi-agent debate/voting is one of the most common 'add more agents to cross-check the answer' design patterns, and this paper shows the final synthesis step -- the part teams trust the most -- is exactly where fabricated consensus hides, with a peer-reviewed, statistically significant human-preference finding that users want honest failure over fake fluency
